name: Critical Thinking and Decision Making
description: Reasoning well at work: logical fallacies, cognitive biases, argument structure, evaluating evidence, modes of reasoning, decision tools, questioning, statistical thinking, problem framing and communicating reasoning.

cards.subject: Ad hominem
says: attacks the person making a claim instead of the claim
ignores whether the argument itself holds
cards.use: hear a point dismissed because of who said it

cards.subject: Straw man
says: misrepresents someone's position to make it easier to attack
rebuts a claim the other person never made
cards.use: hear your view restated in an exaggerated form and then refuted

cards.subject: False dilemma
says: presents two options as the only ones when others exist
pushes a choice by hiding alternatives
cards.use: are told it is either this plan or disaster

cards.subject: Slippery slope
says: claims one step will inevitably lead to an extreme outcome without showing the chain
substitutes fear of the end point for evidence
cards.use: hear that a small change will inevitably lead to catastrophe

cards.subject: Appeal to authority
says: treats a claim as true because an authority said so
fails when the authority is outside their field of expertise
cards.use: hear a claim defended only by the title of the person making it

cards.subject: Circular reasoning
says: uses the conclusion as one of its own premises
proves nothing because it assumes what it sets out to show
cards.use: notice an argument ends up where it started

cards.subject: Post hoc fallacy
says: assumes that because B followed A, A caused B
confuses sequence with cause
cards.use: hear that sales fell after the new logo so the logo caused it

cards.subject: Bandwagon appeal
says: claims something is right because many people believe or do it
mistakes popularity for evidence
cards.use: hear everyone is using it as the reason to adopt a tool

cards.subject: Red herring
says: introduces an irrelevant point to divert attention from the issue
changes the subject without answering
cards.use: see a question answered with an unrelated topic

cards.subject: Hasty generalisation
says: draws a broad conclusion from too few or unrepresentative cases
treats one or two examples as the rule
cards.use: hear a rule drawn from a couple of customer complaints

cards.subject: Tu quoque
says: dismisses criticism by pointing to the critic's own faults
does not address whether the criticism is correct
cards.use: hear you are one to talk as a reply to a valid criticism

cards.subject: Confirmation bias
says: favours information that agrees with existing beliefs
discounts evidence that contradicts them
cards.use: notice you only read sources that agree with you

cards.subject: Anchoring bias
says: lets the first number seen pull later estimates toward it
affects negotiations and estimates
cards.use: find a first quoted figure shaping everyone's later guesses

cards.subject: Availability heuristic
says: judges likelihood by how easily examples come to mind
overstates vivid or recent events
cards.use: overrate a risk because of a recent news story

cards.subject: Survivorship bias
says: studies only the cases that survived a selection process
ignores the failures that are no longer visible
cards.use: learn from the habits of successful companies and ignore those that failed

cards.subject: Hindsight bias
says: makes an outcome seem predictable after it is known
distorts reviews of past decisions
cards.use: hear I knew it all along after an incident

cards.subject: Overconfidence bias
says: rates one's own accuracy higher than results justify
narrows the ranges in estimates
cards.use: give a range that turns out too narrow most of the time

cards.subject: Framing effect
says: changes a choice by presenting the same facts as gain or loss
shows that wording alters decisions
cards.use: see a choice change when 90 percent survive becomes 10 percent die

cards.subject: Groupthink
says: suppresses dissent to preserve group harmony
leads a cohesive team to agree on a poor decision
cards.use: see a team agree quickly and nobody raise doubts

cards.subject: Planning fallacy
says: underestimates time and cost even when past projects overran
favours the best-case plan over past experience
cards.use: estimate a project from the best case again

cards.subject: Halo effect
says: lets one good trait colour the judgement of unrelated traits
inflates ratings of a person who impressed in one area
cards.use: rate a candidate highly on everything because of one strong answer

cards.subject: Loss aversion
says: weights a loss more heavily than an equal gain
makes people hold on to losing positions
cards.use: see a team keep a failing project to avoid admitting the loss

cards.subject: Premise
says: is a statement offered as support for a conclusion
can be true or false independently of the argument's form
cards.use: need to identify what an argument is relying on

cards.subject: Conclusion
says: is the claim an argument tries to establish
follows from the premises if the argument works
cards.use: need to find the point an argument is making

cards.subject: Valid argument
says: has a conclusion that must be true if the premises are true
is about logical form rather than the truth of the premises
cards.use: check whether a conclusion follows from the premises

cards.subject: Sound argument
says: is valid and has all true premises
guarantees a true conclusion
cards.use: want an argument you can rely on to reach a true conclusion

cards.subject: Hidden assumption
says: is an unstated premise the argument needs
is found by asking what must be true for the conclusion to follow
cards.use: feel an argument has a gap but cannot say where

cards.subject: Counterexample
says: is a case that meets a claim's conditions but contradicts it
refutes a universal claim with a single instance
cards.use: hear a claim that something is always true

cards.subject: Steelmanning
says: restates the strongest version of an opposing view before answering it
is the opposite of building a straw man
cards.use: want to test your position against its best opponent

cards.subject: Burden of proof
says: rests on the person making a claim
is not met by asking others to disprove it
cards.use: hear someone say prove me wrong in support of their own claim

cards.subject: Necessary condition
says: must be present for an outcome to occur
does not guarantee the outcome on its own
cards.use: ask what must be in place before an outcome is possible

cards.subject: Sufficient condition
says: guarantees the outcome when present
may not be the only way to get that outcome
cards.use: ask what is enough on its own to guarantee a result

cards.subject: Falsifiability
says: requires a claim to state what observation would show it wrong
separates testable claims from unfalsifiable ones
cards.use: hear a claim that no possible result could disprove

cards.subject: Anecdote
says: is a single story offered as proof
is vivid but cannot show how common something is
cards.use: are given one customer story as proof of a trend

cards.subject: Correlation without causation
says: reminds us that two things moving together need not be linked by cause
calls for a controlled test to establish cause
cards.use: see two measures rise together and are tempted to link them

cards.subject: Confounding variable
says: influences both the supposed cause and the effect
creates a link that disappears once it is controlled for
cards.use: find a link that might be explained by a third factor

cards.subject: Controlled experiment
says: changes one factor while holding the others constant
uses a control group for comparison
cards.use: need to show that a change caused a result

cards.subject: Randomisation
says: assigns subjects to groups by chance
spreads unknown differences evenly between groups
cards.use: need groups that differ only by the treatment

cards.subject: Sample size
says: affects how much random variation a result contains
makes small studies unreliable
cards.use: are shown a surprising result from a handful of cases

cards.subject: Selection bias
says: arises when the sample is not representative of the population
happens when who is included depends on the outcome
cards.use: survey only the customers who answered an email

cards.subject: Primary source
says: is the original record or first-hand account
is preferred over a report about it
cards.use: want the original data rather than someone's summary

cards.subject: Secondary source
says: interprets or summarises primary sources
may add error through the writer's own reading
cards.use: are reading a review or summary of the original research

cards.subject: Peer review
says: has independent experts examine research before publication
reduces but does not remove errors
cards.use: want to judge how far to trust a published study

cards.subject: Replication
says: repeats a study to check the result holds
makes a one-off finding more credible
cards.use: see a striking result from a single study

cards.subject: Source reliability check
says: asks who produced a claim, how they know it and what they gain from it
weighs independence and expertise
cards.use: are deciding whether to believe a report

cards.subject: Deductive reasoning
says: draws conclusions that follow necessarily from premises
moves from a general rule to a specific case
cards.use: apply a known rule to a particular case

cards.subject: Inductive reasoning
says: generalises from observed cases to a probable conclusion
never makes the conclusion certain
cards.use: conclude a pattern from repeated observations

cards.subject: Abductive reasoning
says: infers the best explanation for an observation
underlies diagnosis from symptoms
cards.use: have an observation and need the most likely cause

cards.subject: Reasoning by analogy
says: argues that two things alike in some ways are alike in another
is weakened by relevant differences
cards.use: argue that something worked elsewhere so it will work here

cards.subject: First-principles thinking
says: breaks a problem into basic truths and builds up from them
avoids copying what has always been done
cards.use: want to question how a solution is usually built

cards.subject: Inversion
says: asks how to guarantee failure and then avoids it
solves a problem by looking at its opposite
cards.use: find it hard to see how to succeed

cards.subject: Second-order thinking
says: considers the consequences of consequences
exposes side effects that a first-order view misses
cards.use: are about to make a change with knock-on effects

cards.subject: Counterfactual thinking
says: asks what would have happened if a factor had been different
tests whether a factor really mattered
cards.use: want to know whether a decision caused an outcome

cards.subject: Reductio ad absurdum
says: shows a claim false by deriving an absurd result from it
assumes the claim and exposes a contradiction
cards.use: want to show that a claim leads to an impossible result

cards.subject: Bayesian updating
says: revises a belief in proportion to how strongly new evidence supports it
starts from a prior probability
cards.use: need to change your estimate as new evidence arrives

cards.subject: Probabilistic thinking
says: expresses beliefs as likelihoods rather than certainties
accepts that good decisions can have bad outcomes
cards.use: face a decision with uncertain outcomes

cards.subject: Pre-mortem
says: imagines the project has failed and asks why
surfaces risks before they happen
cards.use: want the team to name risks before a launch

cards.subject: Decision matrix
says: scores options against weighted criteria
makes trade-offs explicit
cards.use: must compare several options against several criteria

cards.subject: Reversible decision
says: can be undone cheaply if it proves wrong
deserves speed over long analysis
cards.use: face a choice that can be changed next week at little cost

cards.subject: Irreversible decision
says: is costly or impossible to undo
justifies slower, more careful analysis
cards.use: face a choice that cannot be undone once made

cards.subject: Opportunity cost
says: is the value of the best alternative given up
makes every choice a trade-off
cards.use: choose between two uses of the same time or budget

cards.subject: Expected value
says: weights each outcome by its probability and sums them
helps compare uncertain options
cards.use: must compare options with uncertain payoffs

cards.subject: OODA loop
says: cycles through observe, orient, decide and act
rewards a faster cycle than the other side
cards.use: must decide and act quickly in a changing situation

cards.subject: Devil's advocate
says: argues the opposing case on purpose to test a proposal
is an assigned role rather than the person's own view
cards.use: want a proposal challenged before it is approved

cards.subject: Red team
says: is a group tasked with attacking a plan or system to find weaknesses
goes beyond a single contrarian
cards.use: need an independent attempt to break a plan

cards.subject: Satisficing
says: chooses the first option that meets the criteria
saves effort when the best option is not worth finding
cards.use: face a low-stakes choice with many similar options

cards.subject: Cost-benefit analysis
says: compares the total expected costs and benefits of an option
puts both on a common scale
cards.use: must justify whether an option is worth doing

cards.subject: Socratic questioning
says: probes a claim through a series of questions
exposes assumptions and gaps in reasoning
cards.use: want someone to examine their own reasoning

cards.subject: Clarifying question
says: asks what a term or request means before answering
prevents solving the wrong problem
cards.use: receive a vague request

cards.subject: Asking for evidence
says: asks how we know a claim is true
moves a discussion from opinion to support
cards.use: hear a strong claim with nothing behind it

cards.subject: What would change your mind
says: asks what evidence would make someone revise their position
tests whether a belief is open to evidence
cards.use: suspect a position cannot be shifted by any facts

cards.subject: Open question
says: invites a full answer rather than yes or no
draws out information the asker did not expect
cards.use: want to learn more than a yes or no

cards.subject: Closed question
says: can be answered yes, no or with a single fact
confirms a detail quickly
cards.use: need to confirm one fact

cards.subject: Chesterton's fence
says: says to understand why something exists before removing it
warns against dismantling what you do not understand
cards.use: want to delete a process or rule nobody can explain

cards.subject: Probing assumptions
says: asks what must be true for a plan to work
brings hidden premises into the open
cards.use: are given a plan that depends on things nobody has said

cards.subject: Who benefits
says: asks who gains from a claim or decision
helps spot conflicts of interest
cards.use: hear a recommendation from a party that profits from it

cards.subject: Asking for the baseline
says: asks what a number is being compared with
stops a figure being read without context
cards.use: are told sales rose 20 percent with no comparison

cards.subject: Median
says: is the middle value when data are ordered
resists the effect of outliers
cards.use: have a few extreme values in the data

cards.subject: Mean
says: adds all values and divides by their number
is pulled by extreme values
cards.use: want the arithmetic average

cards.subject: P-value
says: is the probability of data this extreme if the null hypothesis were true
is not the probability that the hypothesis is true
cards.use: read a significance result in a report
not: states the probability that the hypothesis is true

cards.subject: Statistical significance
says: indicates a result is unlikely to be chance alone under a chosen threshold
says nothing about the size or importance of an effect
cards.use: see a result described as significant

cards.subject: Practical significance
says: asks whether an effect is large enough to matter
can be absent even when a result is statistically significant
cards.use: see a tiny effect with a very small p-value

cards.subject: Simpson's paradox
says: reverses a trend when groups are combined
arises from an uneven mix of subgroups
cards.use: see a trend in every subgroup that reverses in the total

cards.subject: Regression to the mean
says: moves extreme results back toward average on remeasurement
makes a chosen worst performer look improved without any action
cards.use: see the lowest scorers improve on retest after a training course

cards.subject: Base rate fallacy
says: ignores how common something is when judging a test result
makes a positive result for a rare condition seem more certain than it is
cards.use: read a positive result from an accurate test for a rare condition

cards.subject: Confidence interval
says: gives a range likely to contain the true value
widens when there is more uncertainty
cards.use: want to know how precise an estimate is

cards.subject: Goodhart's law
says: states that a measure used as a target stops being a good measure
explains the gaming of metrics
cards.use: see a team improve a number without improving the outcome

cards.subject: P-hacking
says: tries many analyses until one gives a significant result
produces findings that fail to replicate
cards.use: suspect a result was found by trying many cuts of the data

cards.subject: Problem statement
says: describes the gap between the current and desired state
is written before solutions are proposed
cards.use: start work with the solution already assumed

cards.subject: MECE
says: splits a problem into parts that do not overlap and leave nothing out
keeps an analysis complete without duplication
cards.use: must break a problem into groups without gaps or overlaps

cards.subject: Issue tree
says: breaks a question into branches of sub-questions
shows where to focus analysis
cards.use: face a large question that needs structure

cards.subject: Hypothesis-driven approach
says: states a likely answer early and tests it
saves time over gathering all data first
cards.use: have limited time and a lot of possible data

cards.subject: Constraint
says: is a limit such as time, budget or rule that any solution must respect
shapes which options are viable
cards.use: must list what any solution has to respect

cards.subject: Success criterion
says: defines how you will know the problem is solved
is agreed before work starts
cards.use: want to know when the work is finished

cards.subject: Pareto principle
says: observes that a small share of causes produces most of the effects
helps choose where to focus
cards.use: have many issues and limited time

cards.subject: XY problem
says: occurs when someone asks about their attempted solution instead of the real problem
is resolved by asking what they are trying to achieve
cards.use: receive an odd request for help with a workaround

cards.subject: Scope boundary
says: states what is included and excluded
prevents silent growth of the work
cards.use: see requirements creeping in without agreement

cards.subject: Fermi estimate
says: breaks an unknown quantity into rough, estimable parts
gives an order-of-magnitude answer fast
cards.use: need a rough size for something with no data

cards.subject: Stakeholder map
says: identifies who is affected by or can influence a decision
shows whose needs and objections to consider
cards.use: must plan who to consult before a change

cards.subject: Pyramid principle
says: puts the answer first and supports it with grouped arguments
structures writing top-down
cards.use: write a recommendation for senior readers

cards.subject: Bottom line up front
says: opens a message with the conclusion or request
lets a busy reader act without reading everything
cards.use: write an email that needs a decision

cards.subject: Fact versus opinion
says: separates what can be verified from what is a judgement
stops preferences being treated as facts
cards.use: hear a preference presented as a fact

cards.subject: Observation versus inference
says: separates what was seen from what was concluded from it
stops guesses being reported as events
cards.use: describe what happened in an incident

cards.subject: Confidence statement
says: says how sure you are and why
lets readers weigh a claim appropriately
cards.use: give an estimate or forecast to decision-makers

cards.subject: Disagree and commit
says: lets people argue a decision openly and then back it fully once made
avoids stalled decisions
cards.use: are overruled after having made your case

cards.subject: Decision record
says: writes down a decision, its context and the options rejected
helps later teams understand why
cards.use: make a choice others will later question

cards.subject: Strong opinions, weakly held
says: means arguing a view firmly while changing it quickly on new evidence
combines conviction with openness
cards.use: want to debate firmly without defending a position to the end

cards.subject: Ladder of inference
says: describes how people climb from observed data to beliefs and actions
helps trace a conclusion back to the data
cards.use: want to find where two people's views diverged

cards.subject: Active listening
says: restates what the speaker said to confirm understanding
reduces misreading before replying
cards.use: want to check you understood before answering

cards.subject: Occam's razor
says: prefers the explanation with the fewest assumptions
is a guide, not proof
cards.use: have several explanations that fit the facts

cards.subject: Hanlon's razor
says: suggests not blaming malice for what oversight explains
keeps reactions to mistakes calm
cards.use: see a colleague's action that harmed you and need to interpret it

cards.subject: Hickam's dictum
says: warns that several causes may exist together
argues against assuming a single explanation
cards.use: find that a simple explanation does not account for everything

cards.subject: Map is not the territory
says: reminds that a model is a simplification of reality
warns against trusting a model over observation
cards.use: see a model's output conflict with what you observe

cards.subject: Black swan
says: is a rare, high-impact event that was not predicted
shows the limits of forecasting from past data
cards.use: plan for events outside past experience

cards.subject: Fundamental attribution error
says: explains others' behaviour by character and ignores their situation
makes people blame individuals for system failures
cards.use: are about to blame a person for a failure

cards.subject: Trade-off
says: means gaining one quality costs another
has no option that wins on everything
cards.use: are asked for the best option and none is best on all counts

cards.subject: Reference class forecasting
says: estimates from outcomes of similar past projects
counters the planning fallacy
cards.use: need a realistic estimate for a new project

cards.subject: Premature closure
says: stops considering alternatives after the first plausible answer
is reduced by listing at least two explanations
cards.use: have a first answer and feel ready to stop

qa.q: A manager says we should not trust her analysis because she failed the last project. Which fallacy is this?
qa.right: Ad hominem
qa.why: It attacks the person rather than the analysis.

qa.q: Asked about budget overruns, a director talks about the team's great culture. Which fallacy is this?
qa.right: Red herring
qa.why: The point is irrelevant to the question.

qa.q: Someone says we either adopt this vendor or lose the contract. Which fallacy is this?
qa.right: False dilemma
qa.why: It presents only two options when others exist.

qa.q: Sales dropped after the website redesign, so the redesign must have caused it. What is the flaw?
qa.right: It assumes sequence shows cause
wrong: It uses too large a sample
qa.why: Post hoc reasoning confuses order with cause.

qa.q: Everyone else has moved to this framework, so we should too. What is missing?
qa.right: Evidence that it suits our needs
qa.why: Popularity is not evidence of fit.

qa.q: An argument states that the policy is good because it is the best policy. What is wrong?
qa.right: It is circular
qa.why: The conclusion is used as its own premise.

qa.q: A study finds ice cream sales and drowning rise together. What is the best explanation?
qa.right: A confounding factor such as hot weather
wrong: Pure coincidence is the only possibility
qa.why: A third factor can drive both measures.

qa.q: You review the habits of ten successful founders and conclude their habits cause success. What bias is most likely?
qa.right: Survivorship bias
qa.why: You see only the winners and not the failed founders with the same habits.

qa.q: After a failed launch, a colleague says the signs were obvious. What bias is this?
qa.right: Hindsight bias
qa.why: Outcomes seem predictable once known.

qa.q: A supplier quotes 100,000 first and a later offer of 70,000 feels cheap. What is at work?
qa.right: Anchoring bias
qa.why: The first number shapes the perceived value of later ones.

qa.q: Your team has overrun its last four projects and estimates the next one on the best case. What is this?
qa.right: The planning fallacy
qa.why: Past overruns are ignored.

qa.q: A team votes unanimously in five minutes with no questions. What risk should you consider?
qa.right: Groupthink
qa.why: Fast unanimity can mean dissent is being suppressed.

qa.q: A new hire gave a brilliant answer in one interview and is now rated top on every skill. What is this?
qa.right: The halo effect
qa.why: One strength colours unrelated ratings.

qa.q: Which argument is valid but not sound?
qa.right: All birds can fly; a penguin is a bird; therefore a penguin can fly
wrong: All birds have feathers; a robin is a bird; so a robin has feathers
Some birds fly; so all birds fly
Penguins swim; so penguins are fish
qa.why: The form is valid but a premise is false.

qa.q: A team says all users want dark mode, based on three emails. What do you ask first?
qa.right: How many users were asked and how were they chosen
qa.why: Sample size and selection decide how far the claim holds.

qa.q: A result has p = 0.03. What does it mean?
qa.right: If there were no effect, data this extreme would occur about 3 percent of the time
wrong: There is a 97 percent chance the effect is real
qa.why: The p-value is conditional on the null hypothesis.

qa.q: A drug works with p = 0.001 but extends life by two hours on average. What do you conclude?
qa.right: It is statistically significant but may have little practical value
qa.why: Significance does not measure the size of an effect.

qa.q: The worst-performing salespeople improve next quarter without any intervention. What is the likely reason?
qa.right: Regression to the mean
qa.why: Extreme results tend to move toward average.

qa.q: A test is 99 percent accurate for a condition that affects 1 in 10,000 people. A random person tests positive. What matters most?
qa.right: The base rate of the condition
qa.why: A rare condition means most positives are false.

qa.q: A metric becomes a bonus target and staff find ways to inflate it. Which principle is this?
qa.right: Goodhart's law
qa.why: A measure used as a target stops being a good measure.

qa.q: The team tries twenty subgroup analyses and publishes the one with p below 0.05. What is this?
qa.right: P-hacking
qa.why: Many tries make a chance result likely.

qa.q: Which design best shows that a new onboarding flow increases retention?
qa.right: Randomly assign new users to old or new flow and compare
wrong: Compare this month to last month
Look at the best three users
qa.why: Randomisation and a control group isolate the effect of the change.

qa.q: A project is a one-way door. What does this suggest about the decision process?
qa.right: Spend more time analysing before committing
qa.why: Irreversible decisions justify more care.

qa.q: Before launch you ask the team to imagine it has failed in six months and write why. What is this?
qa.right: A pre-mortem
qa.why: It surfaces risks before they occur.

qa.q: You can spend a week on option A or option B. What is the opportunity cost of choosing A?
qa.right: The value of B that you give up
qa.why: Opportunity cost is the best alternative forgone.

qa.q: An option pays 100 with probability 0.2 and 10 otherwise. What is its expected value?
Your colleague argues for the opposite of a plan just to test it. What is the role?
qa.right: Devil's advocate
qa.why: The role is assigned to test the plan.

qa.q: A team wants to delete a rarely used approval step nobody can explain. What should they do first?
qa.right: Find out why it was introduced
qa.why: Chesterton's fence says to understand it before removing it.

qa.q: A sales chart reports growth of 20 percent. What is the best first question?
qa.right: Compared with what, and over which period?
qa.why: Without a baseline the figure has no meaning.

qa.q: A client asks how to remove the last three characters of every file name. What is the best response?
qa.right: Ask what they are trying to achieve
qa.why: They may be asking about a workaround rather than the real problem.

qa.q: You must tell a busy executive that a project will be late. How should the message start?
qa.right: With the conclusion and what is needed from them
qa.why: Lead with the answer and request.

qa.q: Which statement is an observation rather than an inference?
qa.right: The deployment finished at 14:03
qa.why: It records what was seen, not a conclusion.

qa.q: A colleague missed a deadline. Before concluding they are careless, what should you consider?
qa.right: Their situation and constraints
qa.why: The fundamental attribution error overlooks the situation.

qa.q: Which is the strongest reason to use reference class forecasting?
qa.right: It uses outcomes of similar past projects to correct optimism
wrong: It lets you pick the best case
qa.why: It counters the planning fallacy.

qa.q: Which is a good approach to a problem with several possible explanations?
qa.right: List at least two explanations and test which fits
qa.why: Listing alternatives avoids premature closure.

qa.q: You are given a plan that depends on suppliers delivering on time. Which question helps most?
qa.right: What must be true for the plan to work?
qa.why: It surfaces hidden assumptions.

qa.q: A person says nothing could change their mind about a theory. What is the problem?
qa.right: The claim is not falsifiable
qa.why: A claim that no observation could refute cannot be tested.

qa.q: Which is the best way to split a market-sizing problem into groups?
qa.right: MECE categories with no overlap and no gaps
qa.why: MECE keeps coverage complete without double-counting.

qa.q: You are asked how many piano tuners are in a city, with no data. What is the best approach?
qa.right: Break it into rough estimable parts
qa.why: A Fermi estimate builds a rough answer from parts.

qa.q: A decision has been made against your advice. What does disagree and commit mean?
qa.right: Support it fully after having argued your case
qa.why: The group moves on once it has decided.

qa.q: You find you only click on articles that agree with you. What should you do?
qa.right: Seek out the strongest opposing evidence
qa.why: This counters confirmation bias.

qa.q: A manager rates a report highly on teamwork because the report is brilliant technically. What is it?
qa.right: The halo effect
qa.why: One trait influences unrelated ratings.

qa.q: A pilot succeeded in a team of five. Someone says it will work across 5,000 staff. What is the best question?
qa.right: How representative was the pilot group?
wrong: How long was the slide deck?
qa.why: Generalising requires a representative sample.

qa.q: Two explanations fit the evidence equally well; one needs more assumptions. Which does Occam's razor favour?
qa.right: The one with fewer assumptions
qa.why: It is a guide to prefer the simpler explanation.

qa.q: After a bug, the team blames Jane. A systems view suggests what?
qa.right: Look at the conditions that let the error through
wrong: Add a new rule for Jane
qa.why: Blaming the individual overlooks systemic causes.

qa.q: A source provides a bold claim and profits from its adoption. What do you do?
qa.right: Weigh the claim with the conflict of interest in mind and seek independent evidence
qa.why: Conflicts of interest reduce independence, not necessarily accuracy.

qa.q: A project has a clear end state but no agreed way to tell when it is done. What is missing?
qa.right: Success criteria
qa.why: Success criteria define when the work is finished.
